```{r data, include=FALSE}
diamonds <- read.csv("diamonds.csv")
dim(diamonds)
head(diamonds)
str(diamonds)
```

# 1. Research Question and Objective

Question: Which diamond characteristics are the strongest predictors of price?

Imagine you're a diamond merchant traveling to South Africa to inspect diamonds before making a purchase. Due to time constraints, meticulously evaluating every single characteristic of each diamond may be impractical. Therefore, understanding which factors are most helpful in predicting prices will help diamond merchants make faster and more informed decisions.

This study aims to identify the most useful characteristics for predicting diamond prices, including carat weight, cut, color, clarity, and physical dimensions. We will use MLR to study the relationship between these characteristics and diamond prices, and to determine which predictive factors provide the most valuable price information.

# 2. Exploratory Data Analysis

```{r check_z, include=FALSE}
# check if any diamond has z = 0
diamonds[diamonds$z == 0, ]
```

### 2.1 Distribution of Diamond Prices

This histogram shows the distribution of diamond prices in our dataset. It helps us understand the overall price range, identify possible skewness, and check for unusually high or low prices.
```{r price_histogram}

# Graph 1: Histogram of Diamond Prices
# This graph shows the distribution of diamond prices.

library(ggplot2)

ggplot(diamonds, aes(x = price)) +
  geom_histogram(bins = 30, fill = "blue", color = "black") +
  labs(title = "Distribution of Diamond Prices",
       x = "Price",
       y = "Frequency")
```

The diamond price distribution is right-skewed, with the majority of diamonds concentrated in the lower price range. The average price ($4,221.30) is higher than the median ($2,594), indicating that a small number of high-priced diamonds have artificially inflated the average price. This skewed distribution warrants consideration when constructing regression models.

### 2.2 Relationship Between Carat and Price

This scatter plot shows the relationship between diamond weight and price. It helps us examine whether heavier diamonds tend to have higher prices and whether the relationship appears to be linear.

```{r carat_price}

# Graph 2: Scatter Plot of Carat vs Price
# Each point represents one diamond.
# The red line shows the fitted linear trend.

ggplot(diamonds, aes(x = carat, y = price)) +
  geom_point(color = "blue", alpha = 0.5) +
  geom_smooth(method = "lm", se = FALSE, color = "red") +
  labs(title = "Carat vs Price",
       x = "Carat",
       y = "Price (USD)")
```

The scatter plot shows a significant positive correlation between carat weight and diamond price. The correlation coefficient is approximately 0.928, indicating that heavier diamonds generally command higher prices. However, even diamonds with similar carat weights can have price differences, suggesting that other factors may also influence price variations.

### 2.3 Diamond Price by Quality Characteristics

These three boxplots compare diamond prices across three quality characteristics: cut, color, and clarity. The boxplots allow us to compare median prices, price variation, and possible outliers across different quality grades.

```{r quality_price, fig.width=10, fig.height=4, out.width="100%"}
# Graph 3: Diamond Price by Quality Characteristics
# This graph combines Cut, Color, and Clarity boxplots.
# Each panel represents a different quality characteristic.
# Compare price distributions across quality grades.

# Combine the three quality variables into one dataset
quality_data <- data.frame(
  price = rep(diamonds$price, 3),
  grade = c(diamonds$cut, diamonds$color, diamonds$clarity),
  type = rep(c("Cut", "Color", "Clarity"),
             each = nrow(diamonds))
)

# Create three boxplots in one figure
ggplot(quality_data, aes(x = grade, y = price)) +
  geom_boxplot(fill = "blue") +
  facet_wrap(~ type, scales = "free_x", nrow = 1) +
  labs(title = "Diamond Price by Quality Characteristics",
       x = "Quality Grade",
       y = "Price (USD)") +
  theme(axis.text.x = element_text(angle = 45, hjust = 1))
```

Box plots show the price distribution differences across different cut, color, and clarity grades. Interestingly, higher quality grades don't always correlate with higher median prices. For example, in this dataset, the median price of an ideal cut diamond is lower than that of a well cut diamond. This may be partly attributed to the differences in carat weight across different quality grades. MLR can help us further analyze these characteristics while controlling for other predictor variables.

## 3. Initial Multiple Linear Regression and Residual Analysis

### 3.1 Initial Regression Model

In our initial model, we selected six predictor variables: carat, cut, color, clarity, depth, and table.

We don't want to use physical dimensions (x, y, z) because they are highly correlated with carat, which could lead to multicollinearity and make the coefficients difficult to interpret.

Our initial regression model is:

Price ~ Carat + Cut + Color + Clarity + Depth + Table

This model allows us to examine the relationship between diamond characteristics and price while controlling for other predictor variables.


```{r initial_model, include=FALSE}
# Model 1: Initial Multiple Linear Regression.

# Convert variables into factors
diamonds$cut <- factor(diamonds$cut)
diamonds$color <- factor(diamonds$color)
diamonds$clarity <- factor(diamonds$clarity)

# Fit the initial MLR
model1 <- lm(price ~ carat + cut + color + clarity + depth + table,
             data = diamonds)

# Rregression results
summary(model1)
```

### 3.2 Initial Regression Results

```{r model_results}
# This table shows the overall fit of our initial model.
# Use R-squared and adjusted R-squared to evaluate model fit.
# Residual standard error measures the size of the residuals.

model_summary <- summary(model1)

results <- data.frame(
  Statistic = c("R-squared",
                "Adjusted R-squared",
                "Residual Standard Error"),
  Value = c(round(model_summary$r.squared, 4),
            round(model_summary$adj.r.squared, 4),
            round(model_summary$sigma, 2))
)

knitr::kable(results)
```

### 3.3 Residual Diagnostics

#### 3.3.1 Residuals vs Fitted

This plot check whether the residuals show any patterns and whether their spread stays approximately constant across fitted values.

```{r residual_plot, fig.width=6, fig.height=3.5, out.width='75%', fig.align='center'}
# Graph 6: Residuals vs Fitted
# X-axis: Predicted diamond prices
# Y-axis: Residuals (actual price - predicted price)
# We use this graph to check linearity and constant variance.

# Get fitted values and residuals from Model 1
res_data <- data.frame(
  fitted = fitted(model1),
  residuals = resid(model1)
)

# Plot residuals against fitted values
ggplot(res_data, aes(x = fitted, y = residuals)) +
  geom_point(color = "blue", alpha = 0.5) +
  geom_hline(yintercept = 0, color = "red") +
  labs(title = "Residuals vs Fitted",
       x = "Fitted Values",
       y = "Residuals")
```

#### 3.3.2 Normal Q-Q Plot

This plot compares the distribution of model residuals with a normal distribution. It helps us check whether the normality assumption is reasonable.

```{r qq_plot, fig.width=6, fig.height=3.5, out.width='75%', fig.align='center'}
# Graph 7: Normal Q-Q Plot
# X-axis: Theoretical normal quantiles
# Y-axis: Sample quantiles of residuals
# We use this graph to check the normality of residuals.

# Plot the residual quantiles
ggplot(res_data, aes(sample = residuals)) +
  stat_qq(color = "blue", alpha = 0.5) +
  stat_qq_line(color = "red") +
  labs(title = "Normal Q-Q Plot",
       x = "Theoretical Quantiles",
       y = "Sample Quantiles")
```
